problem.title: Hosting an open-source monorepo
problem.context: An open-source foundation hosts a 12-year, 40 GB monorepo for about 2,000 contributors across five continents. Most clones come from CI and first-time contributors who need only the latest version. Four volunteers operate donated servers in Europe and North America.

requirements.text: Accept pushes from the maintainers to a single canonical repository over the standard Git protocol.
Let a first-time contributor start working without downloading the whole history.
A contributor in Asia or South America clones the latest version within two minutes on a 50 Mbit/s connection.
A CI job that starts after a push has been accepted always fetches that push.
Four volunteers run the service in their spare time.

points.description: 1. Plain Git repositories on server disks remain authoritative, with one file server serializing reference updates. Paired machines replicate those files block-by-block, while regional caches serve reads and clients use partial clone with sparse checkout to limit transferred data. 2. **Trade-off:** This combines simple authority and atomic updates with reduced client bandwidth and geographically local reads. It gives up the assurance of an accepted durability strategy—the selected block-level replication is marked rejected—and adds cache/origin coordination concerns.

The file server stores each repository as a plain Git repository on its local disk, which is the authoritative state. That same server handles reference updates serially, so concurrent pushes are ordered and each update is applied atomically. Trade-off: This is simple to implement and provides clear consistency without distributed coordination. It gives up update throughput and horizontal availability, since the server and its disks are a central bottleneck and failure point.

The system lets developers create a standard Git working copy using partial clone and sparse checkout. It fetches only the repository history and files needed for the selected work, while retaining normal Git workflows. Trade-off: This reduces download time, bandwidth, and local storage for large repositories. It gives up a complete local dataset, so operations requiring omitted history or files may require additional fetching.

Regional or office cache servers handle fetches, clones, and CI checkouts close to users. On a cache miss, the local server forwards the request to the origin, stores the returned objects, and serves subsequent reads locally. Trade-off: This reduces latency and origin bandwidth for repeated reads, especially across distant offices. It adds cache storage and operational complexity, and cached objects may be stale or require invalidation before clients see newer data.

The system lets developers use standard Git to fetch a repository’s complete history over the Git protocol. After the full clone, they can work with the repository locally using normal Git operations. Trade-off: This provides broad Git compatibility and complete local history, but increases download time, network use, and client storage, especially for large repositories.

A designated server keeps plain Git repositories as the authoritative state, serializes reference updates, and propagates each write to three replicas, acknowledging it after a majority has the change. Regional cache servers serve fetches and clones, forwarding misses to the origin, while clients use partial clone and sparse checkout to obtain only needed data. Trade-off: This provides durable writes, ordered reference updates, reduced read latency, and lower client transfer. Trade-off: Replication and cache consistency add operational complexity, while the single coordinating server can become a throughput or availability bottleneck.

1. Each server stores repository objects and references as plain Git repositories on its local disk, providing the persistent repository state. A reference update is proposed and committed through three-phase commit, with all replicas voting so their local repositories apply the update atomically and in a consistent order. 2. Trade-off: This provides coordinated, durable updates across replicas while retaining simple on-disk Git storage. It adds coordination, latency, and susceptibility to distributed-transaction failures or unavailable replicas during updates.

trajectory.hypothesis: The complete design combines a canonical on-disk Git origin, serial pushes, paired disk replication, partial clone with sparse checkout, and regional caches.

tradeoffs.note: Partial transfer and regional reads help distant contributors start quickly, but the design gives no measured evidence that the two-minute target is met; this records the unresolved target as a partial cost.

trajectory.observation: The point supports canonical Git writes, serialized reference updates, a reduced-transfer contributor path, and geographically local reads. The space marks block-level replication rejected. Partial clone and regional caches make the two-minute target more plausible, but the design supplies no measured clone time; that target remains unproven. CI reads the origin directly, so the cache webhook delay does not affect Q2. C1 is not assessed by a design-space dimension.

trajectory.hypothesis: R1 and Q2 explain the canonical on-disk origin and its serialized reference updates: maintainers have one standard Git destination, and accepted pushes become ordered origin state for CI to fetch.
trajectory.observation: Git at any scale attests this combination. The single origin is the canonical push endpoint, and serialization gives CI a stable, ordered source after acceptance. These requirements call for a canonical, consistent authority but do not establish that local disks or single-server serialization are the only way to provide it.

trajectory.hypothesis: R2 and Q1 explain partial clone with sparse checkout because contributors need to begin without downloading 40 GB and the target connection is only 50 Mbit/s.

tradeoffs.note: The smaller initial transfer meets the no-full-history need, but the quantitative two-minute clone target remains only partly established.

trajectory.observation: Scalar philosophy and Introducing Scalar attest this transfer approach. It directly satisfies the reduced-history intent, and reduces data transferred for the stated large repository. No clone-size or timing measurement proves the two-minute target, so Q1 is supported but unproven rather than a demonstrated miss.

trajectory.hypothesis: Q1 explains placing read caches near contributors in Asia and South America to reduce distance and repeat-transfer time.
trajectory.observation: Introducing Scalar attests regional cache servers, and the region matches the solution's topology. Nearby caches can reduce read latency and origin bandwidth, but the workspace has no measured regional clone time. The point's warning about stale cached objects is addressed in this solution by origin webhooks; the CI path bypasses caches and reads the origin.

trajectory.hypothesis: Test whether R2 and Q1 force partial clone by replacing it with a full clone over Git.
trajectory.observation: The full-clone alternative misses the no-full-history requirement and cannot meet the stated time bound for a 40 GB repository on the stated connection. The partial-clone choice is forced by R2 and Q1 among these compared transfer values.

trajectory.hypothesis: Test the solution's block-level replication against an accepted three-replica majority-write alternative; the explicit requirements do not state a durability target, but this may reveal whether the volunteer constraint distinguishes the choices.

tradeoffs.note: Partial transfer helps first-time contributors start without the full history, but the two-minute performance result remains unmeasured; the durability contrast does not resolve that target.

trajectory.observation: The three-replica combination is attested as a whole, while the solution's block-level replication is rejected by the sources that discuss it. The named requirements do not say how much durability is required or compare its operational burden for four volunteers; C1 has no matching dimension. Therefore the design space does not establish that the solution's replication choice is forced, and its own evidence is adverse.

trajectory.hypothesis: Test whether Q2 forces one-server serialization by replacing it with three-phase commit across replicas while retaining the on-disk repository authority.
trajectory.observation: Three-phase commit is also attested with local Git repositories, and the point supports ordered, atomic updates across replicas. Q2 does not distinguish it from serialization at the origin. The solution's simpler single-server choice is therefore free relative to R1 and Q2; the space does not evaluate its fit with the four-volunteer constraint.

regions.name: Canonical serialized origin
regions.reason: A single authoritative Git repository accepts maintainer pushes, and serialization provides the ordered state that direct-origin CI fetches after push acceptance. The requirements support this region, although they do not force its particular storage and coordination mechanisms.

regions.name: Reduced contributor transfer
regions.reason: Partial clone and sparse checkout let first-time contributors work without a full history and reduce transfer for a very large repository. The alternative full clone misses R2 and the arithmetic rules it out for Q1; actual performance still needs measurement.

regions.name: Regional read caches
regions.reason: Caches near distant contributors support lower read latency. This is consistent with Q1 but the two-minute target is unproven, and this value alone does not describe the cache webhook or direct-origin CI path.

alternatives.name: Monorepo hosting as built
alternatives.summary: A central on-disk Git origin serializes pushes and has a manually activated disk replica. Regional caches serve most reads, while contributor guidance uses partial clone and sparse checkout. CI reads the origin directly.

choices.reason: The local Git repository is the canonical push destination and stable CI source. The requirements need a canonical authority but do not force local disk as its implementation.
choices.solution_quote: It holds the repository as a plain Git repository on its local disk

choices.reason: The paired disk copy supports manual takeover, but no requirement sets a durability target or distinguishes this choice. Its value is rejected by the sources in the space that discuss it, so it is a solution choice without evidence support in this model.
choices.solution_quote: A second server in the same data centre receives a block-by-block copy of the origin's disk and can take over by hand if the origin fails

choices.reason: Serialization makes accepted pushes visible in a stable order, but the three-phase-commit contrast also supports Q2. The requirements do not force the simpler coordination mechanism.
choices.solution_quote: applies pushes one at a time

choices.reason: It avoids requiring a full-history download and is supported for reducing transfer. The full-clone contrast misses both R2 and the quantitative Q1 bound.
choices.solution_quote: clone with a blob filter and a sparse checkout of the directories they work on

choices.reason: Regional caches support reads closer to contributors, but no measured result establishes the two-minute target and no contrast establishes that this cache design is necessary. CI's direct-origin route and cache update webhook are not represented by this value.
choices.solution_quote: Cache servers in North America, Asia and South America serve clones and fetches

adrs.title: Canonical repository and push ordering
adrs.context: Maintainers need one standard Git push destination, and CI starting after an accepted push must fetch that state. The design uses the origin as the authority and serializes its updates; CI bypasses caches and fetches the origin.

options.name: On-disk origin with serialized updates
pros: Provides one canonical Git repository and a clearly ordered state for direct CI reads.
cons: Makes writes and reads dependent on one server and its local storage.
options.reason: Chosen to provide the requested canonical endpoint and a stable post-acceptance state. Serialization is free relative to Q2 because three-phase commit also meets it.

options.name: On-disk origin with three-phase commit
pros: Coordinates atomic ordered updates across replicas.
cons: Adds distributed coordination and its availability/latency costs.
options.reason: The contrast also meets R1 and Q2, so the requirements do not force the chosen single-server coordination.

adrs.title: Repository durability and manual failover
adrs.context: The design keeps a second copy of the origin disk and allows hand takeover. This supports keeping the canonical repository available after origin failure, which bears on CI fetching accepted state; the stated requirements do not set a recovery-time target, and the space does not assess volunteer workload.

options.name: Paired block-level disk copy
pros: Provides a second disk copy and a manual takeover path.
cons: The space marks this approach rejected in the sources that discuss it.
options.reason: This is a free choice relative to Q2 while the origin is healthy and CI fetches directly from it. The sources in the space argue against this replication approach, and its manual recovery fit is not established.

options.name: Three Git replicas with majority writes
pros: The space attests this durability approach and the evaluated combination.
cons: Its operational burden for this four-volunteer team is not assessed by the space.
options.reason: This attested alternative could preserve accepted updates across replicas, but the requirements do not force majority replication and the space does not compare its volunteer workload.

adrs.title: Contributor clone size
adrs.context: A first-time contributor must start without downloading the full history, and a contributor on a 50 Mbit/s connection has a two-minute latest-version target for a 40 GB monorepo.

options.name: Partial clone with sparse checkout
pros: Avoids requiring all history and limits transferred files to the contributor's work area.
cons: The design reports no measurements proving the two-minute target; omitted objects may need later fetching.
options.reason: The requirements force a reduced-transfer approach over full clone; the exact target still needs a measured clone result.

options.name: Full clone over Git
pros: Leaves the complete history available locally.
cons: Requires the full-history download and 40 GB exceeds the 750 MB theoretical two-minute transfer ceiling at 50 Mbit/s.
options.reason: It misses R2 and Q1, so it cannot replace partial transfer for this problem.

adrs.title: Regional read serving
adrs.context: Contributors far from the European origin need the latest version quickly. Regional caches can serve repeated objects nearby, while the solution uses webhooks after pushes and directs CI to the origin.

options.name: Cache servers near clients
pros: Reduces read distance and can serve repeated objects locally.
cons: Requires cache operations and freshness management; no timing result proves Q1.
options.reason: Chosen as a plausible contributor-latency aid, not as a proven two-minute guarantee. The precise webhook and CI routing are not captured by this value.

uncovered.decision: Origin-triggered webhook refresh of every regional cache after each push
uncovered.solution_quote: After every push, the origin calls a webhook on each cache so that it fetches the new state, which usually takes a few seconds.

uncovered.decision: CI jobs bypass caches and fetch directly from the origin
uncovered.solution_quote: CI jobs are configured to fetch from the origin directly.

uncovered.decision: Nightly full-history Git bundle distribution from caches
uncovered.solution_quote: Every night the origin also writes a Git bundle of the full history, which the caches offer for clones that need everything.

uncovered.decision: Release source tarball publication through a content delivery network
uncovered.solution_quote: For every release tag, a script builds a source tarball and publishes it on a content delivery network, so that packagers download releases without using Git at all.

unaddressed.note: The space has durability replication choices but no dimension or value that assesses routine operational workload, manual recovery effort, or whether four spare-time volunteers can run the design.
